title: The gold (serving) layer
summary: Shaping data for its consumers: marts, aggregates and serving tables for BI, ML and reverse ETL, with the right materialisation, freshness SLAs and naming.

blocks.text: Gold is the product the data platform ships. Its tables are shaped around **consumers and questions**, not around sources: a finance revenue mart, a churn feature table, a customer table synced to the CRM. Silver (chapter 14) guarantees correctness of entities; gold guarantees usefulness, stability and performance for a named audience.

head: Gold artefact
Shape
Main consumer
rows: Semantic layer, BI, ad hoc analysis
Facts pre-summarised to a coarser grain (daily by store)
One row per entity per as-of date, many features
One row per object in the target app, target field names

blocks.text: Business logic that defines what the company means by a term (*net revenue*, *active customer*) should be written once, either in a conformed gold model or in the semantic layer, never re-implemented per dashboard.

layers.label: Gold
layers.sub: marts, aggregates, feature and sync tables

blocks.text: A **mart** is a subject-oriented set of gold models, usually per business domain: `finance`, `marketing`, `operations`. Marts reuse the same conformed dimensions; they differ in which facts and derived models they expose. Domain teams often own their mart while the platform team owns shared dimensions.

**Aggregate tables** trade flexibility for speed. A dashboard scanning 3 billion order lines on every page load costs real money; a daily store-by-category aggregate of 2 million rows answers the same questions in milliseconds. Keep only additive measures (and components of ratios, chapter 8) in aggregates so they can be rolled up further.

blocks.title: Daily sales aggregate (Snowflake)
blocks.text:
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold.agg_sales_daily_store_category AS
SELECT d.full_date            AS sales_date,
       s.store_key,
       p.category_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT f.order_number) AS orders,  -- not additive across days!
       SUM(f.quantity)                AS units,
       SUM(f.net_amount)              AS net_revenue,
       SUM(f.gross_amount)            AS gross_revenue
FROM gold.fct_order_line f
JOIN gold.dim_date    d ON f.order_date_key = d.date_key
JOIN gold.dim_product p ON f.product_key    = p.product_key
JOIN gold.dim_store   s ON f.store_key      = s.store_key
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;

Distinct counts are not additive: summing daily distinct orders per category gives the wrong weekly total when one order spans several categories. Either compute distinct counts at the target grain, or store sketches (HyperLogLog, for example Snowflake's `HLL_ACCUMULATE` and `HLL_COMBINE`) that can be merged approximately.
15.3 Serving ML, reverse ETL and applications

items: **ML feature tables**: one row per entity and as-of timestamp, built with point-in-time joins (chapter 9) to avoid leakage. Training reads history; batch scoring reads the latest snapshot. Feature definitions in gold should match those served online, or models see different data in production.

**Reverse ETL**: tools sync gold tables into SaaS applications (lead scores into the CRM, segments into the email tool). Shape the table exactly like the target object, keep a stable primary key, and only expose changed rows to limit API usage.

**Application serving**: product dashboards and APIs need predictable millisecond latency and high concurrency. Warehouses are usually not the right serving tier for thousands of queries per second; publish from gold into a cache, an OLAP database or the application database instead (chapter 46).

blocks.text: Once gold feeds operational systems, it is production. A broken reverse-ETL table can overwrite thousands of CRM records. Apply the same change control, tests and alerting as for application code, and prefer sync tools with dry runs and row-change limits.

head: Materialisation
Freshness
Query cost
Use when
rows: Cheap logic, low traffic, or thin renaming layer
Small to medium models, logic changes often
Cheap to read, cheap to build
Large facts with append or upsert patterns
Cheap to read; engine pays refresh
Simple aggregates the engine supports incrementally

blocks.text: The usual default in dbt projects: views or ephemeral models for staging, tables for marts, incremental for large facts. Materialised views and dynamic tables have engine-specific limits on which SQL they can maintain incrementally; check the current documentation before relying on them for complex joins.

Every gold table should have a stated freshness target and an owner, agreed with its consumers. *Finance revenue mart: complete for the previous day by 07:00 UTC, owner finance-data team.* Write it down, and measure it.

items: Monitor freshness with `max(loaded_at)` checks or dbt `source freshness` and table-level observability (chapter 33).
Publish atomically: consumers should see yesterday's complete data or today's complete data, never half of each. Build into a new table and swap, or use write-audit-publish.
Expose a status signal (a last-successful-load table or catalog tag) so dashboards can show *data as of*.

blocks.text: 15.6 Feeding the semantic layer, and naming

The semantic layer (chapters 35-36) defines metrics, dimensions and join paths on top of gold. It works best on clean dimensional marts: facts with declared grain, conformed dimensions with stable keys, additive measures. Leave metric arithmetic (ratios, period comparisons, filters such as *excluding test orders*) to the semantic layer, so every tool gets the same definition. Gold provides the stable ingredients.

blocks.title: From 400 dashboard queries to one mart
blocks.text: A subscription company's BI tool contained about 400 saved queries computing MRR directly on silver, with five different churn definitions. The analytics team built a `gold_finance` mart with `fct_subscription_daily` (periodic snapshot), conformed `dim_customer` and `dim_plan`, and defined MRR and churn once in the semantic layer.
items: Board reporting and product dashboards now agree to the cent
Dashboard compute cost dropped because queries hit a pre-aggregated daily snapshot
A freshness SLA of 06:00 UTC is published and monitored

blocks.title: Design gold for a ride-hailing company
blocks.text: Consumers are: an operations dashboard refreshed every 5 minutes, monthly finance reporting, a driver-churn model, and a sync of rider segments to a marketing tool. Propose the gold tables, their grain, materialisation, freshness SLA, owner and names, and decide which logic lives in gold versus the semantic layer.
hints: Does the 5-minute dashboard need the same tables as finance?
Which consumer would be harmed most by a half-published load?

items: Gold is shaped for named consumers: marts, aggregates, wide tables, feature, reverse-ETL and serving tables.
Aggregates keep additive measures; distinct counts need target-grain computation or mergeable sketches.
Gold feeding operational systems is production and needs production change control.
Choose materialisation by freshness, query cost and build cost; publish atomically.
Every gold table has an owner, a freshness SLA and a predictable name; metric arithmetic belongs in the semantic layer.

blocks.q: A daily aggregate stores `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` per store. A user sums it over a week. What is wrong?
options: The weekly total counts repeat customers several times
Daily grain cannot be rolled up at all
blocks.explain: A customer who buys on three days is counted three times. Distinct counts are non-additive; compute them at weekly grain or use mergeable sketches such as HLL.

blocks.q: Where should the definition of a ratio metric like conversion rate live?
options: Stored as a precomputed percentage column on every gold row
In the semantic layer, computed from additive components in gold
blocks.explain: Gold provides the additive numerator and denominator; the semantic layer computes the ratio after aggregation so every tool gets the same answer. Stored percentages cannot be re-aggregated correctly.

blocks.q: Which materialisation fits a 4 billion-row order-line fact receiving 5 million new or changed rows a day?
blocks.explain: Incremental builds process only the change volume while keeping reads cheap. A view recomputes on every query and an hourly full rebuild reprocesses 4 billion rows each time.

blocks.q: Why is publishing gold atomically important?
options: Consumers never see a mix of partially loaded new data and old data
It removes the need for tests
It is required by SQL standards
blocks.explain: Atomic publishing (swap, write-audit-publish) ensures a dashboard shows either the old complete state or the new complete state, never half-loaded numbers.
